entry.title: The Frontiers in Natural Sciences: The Dean’s Annual Lecture 2026

media:group.media:title: The Frontiers in Natural Sciences: The Dean’s Annual Lecture 2026
media:group.media:description:
The Frontiers in Natural Sciences: The Dean’s Annual Lecture 2026, delivered by Geordie Williamson on the subject of ‘AI and the long conversation of mathematics’.
The lecture was followed by a panel discussion on the current state of AI within Mathematics. Professor Williamson will be joined on the panel by Ulrike Tillmann, Professor of Mathematics at the University of Oxford, Director of the Isaac Newton Institute at the University of Cambridge, and former President of LMS; Ana Caraiani, Royal Society University Research Fellow; and Kevin Buzzard, Professor of Pure Mathematics at Imperial College London.

Cyber-security, healthcare, medical devices, data, patient safety, and finding solutions in emerging technologies.

media:group.media:title: IN-CYPHER Hackathon
media:group.media:description:
On 21 to 22 September 2026, over forty students from NUS, SIT, and NTU competed in the IN-CYPHER Hackathon. Teams built an autonomous AI agent to solve Capture-the-Flag (CTF) challenges spanning categories such as web, pwn, crypto, reversing, forensics and more, with several set in medical and healthcare scenarios.
The event was proudly sponsored by CyberSG R&D Programme Office (CRPO) and comes from IN-CYPHER, a joint Imperial College London & Nanyang Technological University research programme focused on securing the medical systems and healthcare technology people depend on.

entry.title: The look of why: causality matters in medical imaging AI

media:group.media:title: The look of why: causality matters in medical imaging AI
media:group.media:description:
Artificial intelligence has the potential to transform medical imaging, from earlier detection of diseases to more accurate diagnosis. Yet AI systems can fail when faced with new or different data, raising important questions about their reliability, robustness and fairness.
Join Professor Ben Glocker, Professor in Machine Learning for Imaging, to discover why causality matters for understanding when AI works and when it fails, and how ‘what-if’ reasoning could help expose blind spots and build more trustworthy medical imaging AI. #ImperialInaugurals

entry.title: 🔥 Fire built civilizations, but burns may have shaped human evolution.

media:group.media:title: 🔥 Fire built civilizations, but burns may have shaped human evolution.
media:group.media:description:
Research led by Dr Joshua Cuddihy from Imperial Medicine explores how countless small, survivable burn injuries across history could have influenced the way humans heal today.
Discover the surprising link between fire and evolution, and see the video in full over on our YouTube.

entry.title: How did fire shape human evolution? 🔥🧬

media:group.media:title: How did fire shape human evolution? 🔥🧬
media:group.media:description:
For more than a million years, humans have lived alongside fire, using it for cooking, warmth, protection and technological progress. But this uniquely human relationship may also have shaped how our bodies respond to injury.
Research led by Honorary Clinical Research Fellow Dr Josh Cuddihy from the Department of Surgery & Cancer - Faculty of Medicine, published in BioEssays, explores the idea that exposure to burn injuries acted as an evolutionary pressure throughout human history.
The study suggests that repeated, survivable burns may have influenced the evolution of genes involved in wound healing, inflammation and infection response.
By combining expertise in burn medicine, evolutionary biology and genetics, the researchers propose a new perspective on why humans heal the way they do today, and why severe burns can trigger responses that are both protective and harmful.
Find out more:
https://www.imperial.ac.uk/news/articles/medicine/department-of-surgery-and-cancer-news-articles/2026/exposure-to-burn-injuries-played-key-role-in-shaping-human-evolution-study-suggests/

entry.title: Sculpting light in space and time with metamaterials

media:group.media:title: Sculpting light in space and time with metamaterials
media:group.media:description:
Light powers the global internet, enables deep-space and medical imaging, and sustains life on Earth. But how do we control something so fast and intangible?
Join Riccardo Sapienza, Professor of Physics, as he pushes the boundaries of what we can do with light, from metamaterials and ultra-thin lenses to manipulating it in space and time. Can light waves from the past and future interact? Can light scatter from superluminal modulations without breaking relativity? #ImperialInaugurals
